note.explanation: A true solution has solute particles completely mixed into the solvent. Colloidal particles are bigger than true-solution particles, but are too small to see with the naked eye. Suspension particles can be seen, settle if left standing, and are caught by filter paper.
examples: Starch solution is a colloidal solution.
A mixture of chalk in water is a suspension.
note.checkAnswer: A suspension: its particles can be seen, settle on standing, and are caught by filter paper.

steps: Check whether the particles can be seen with the naked eye.

note.answer: A true solution has particles that are not visible and pass through filter paper. A colloid has particles that do not settle and pass through filter paper. A suspension has visible particles that settle and are caught by filter paper.

explain.title: True solution
explain.body: A solution is such a mixture in which solute particles are completely homogenized in the solvent e.g. dissolution of sodium chloride or copper sulphate in water. The solute particles in such a solution cannot be seen by the naked eye. If solution is filtered, these particles pass through the pores of filter paper leaving no residue. Such a solution is called a true solution.

explain.title: Suspension
explain.body: A suspension, on the other hand, is a mixture in which solute particles do not dissolve in the solvent. We can actually see these particles. If a suspension is kept for some time, these particles settle down. Again, if this suspension is filtered, the particles in it cannot pass through the pores of filter paper and can be collected as a residue. A mixture of chalk in water is an example of suspension.

explain.title: Colloidal solution
explain.body: Besides a true solution and a suspension, there is a third form of solution called colloidal solution. In this type, the solute particles do not homogenize with solvent. These particles are a little bit bigger than the solute particles present in the true solution but not big enough to be seen with a naked eye like the particles present in a suspension. If kept for some time, the particles of a colloidal solution do not settle down. On filtration, these particles pass through the filter paper like the particles of a true solution. Starch solution and white of an egg are the common examples of colloidal solutions.

mistakes: Do not say that colloidal particles settle; the section says they do not settle on standing.
Do not say colloidal particles are caught by filter paper; they pass through it.
Do not confuse a true solution with a colloid: both pass through filter paper, but colloidal particles are bigger than true-solution particles.
Do not use chalk in water as an example of a true solution; it is a suspension.
